title: 論語 微子第十八
source: Confucius 孔子 and his disciples, 論語 (the Analects), book 18, 〈微子〉, in the received text as printed in Zhu Xi 朱熹, 論語集注 (part of his 四書章句集注, completed c. 1190), from the Wenyuange 文淵閣 copy of the Siku Quanshu 四庫全書 (1782), as transcribed by the Kanseki Repository (Kanripo, KR1h0015). Collated character by character against two further pre-1930 printings, both transcribed by Kanripo: Ruan Yuan's 1816 Nanchang reprint of the Song edition of 論語注疏 (KR1h0004) and He Yan's 論語集解 in the Sibu Congkan photographic reprint of a Song edition (KR1h0005). Readings that change the sense are noted in the notes; graphic variants (悌 for 弟, 爲 for 為) are not. Zhu Xi's text is substantially the one James Legge printed in The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (Hong Kong, 1861), and the passage numbering is the standard one. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none. Characters are traditional, as the edition prints them (衆, not 眾). Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Any prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same modern Mandarin convention; the exact voice used is recorded in audio/<id>/voice.txt and is fixed for every Chinese text.
about: Book 18 of the Analects, 微子 Wēi zǐ, named, as every book is, from its first words — the Viscount of Wei, half-brother of the last Shang king, who left his tyrannical lord rather than serve him. The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Book 18 has 11 passages, and Zhu Xi says it mostly records when sages and worthies took office and when they withdrew. It opens with three men who answered a bad king in three ways — leaving, enduring slavery, dying for their protest — and Kongzi calls all three humane (18.1). Liuxia Hui, dismissed three times, will not leave his own state (18.2); Kongzi leaves Qi when its duke will not use him, and leaves Lu when its chief minister takes a gift of women musicians and holds no court (18.3–4). Then come the recluses who mock him: the madman of Chu singing to the phoenix (18.5); two men ploughing who will not tell Zilu where the ford is, and Kongzi's answer that he cannot go off to live among the birds and beasts (18.6); and an old man, a bamboo basket slung from the staff on his shoulder, who answers Zilu's question with a gibe — 'who is your master?' — and then gives him a night's lodging (18.7). Seven men of worth who lived out of office are named, the Master passes judgment on six of them, two by two, and says he himself has no fixed 'may' or 'may not' (18.8). The book ends with the musicians of Lu scattering to other states, to the River and to the sea (18.9), the Duke of Zhou's counsel to his son (18.10), and eight officers of Zhou, four pairs of brothers (18.11). Each numbered passage begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
微子去之，
箕子為之奴，
比干諫而死。

morph.gloss: the Viscount of Wei — elder half-brother of Zhou, last king of the Shang
the Viscount of Ji — an uncle of Zhou
Bi Gan — another uncle of Zhou

sentences.i: The Viscount of Wei went away from him; the Viscount of Ji was made his slave; Bi Gan spoke out against him and was put to death.
sentences.n: The book is named 微子 from its opening words. Zhu Xi's heading says it mostly records the comings and goings of sages and worthies, when they took office and when they withdrew (此篇多記聖賢之出處), and counts eleven chapters (凡十一章); our numbers are his. The 之 'him' of the first two clauses — and the man Bi Gan remonstrated with — is Zhou 紂, the last king of the Shang (the Yin), whom the text never names: the reader is expected to know. Zhu Xi: Wei and Ji were the names of two states, and 子 is the rank of viscount (微箕二國名子爵也); the Viscount of Wei was Zhou's elder brother by a lesser wife (紂庶兄), the Viscount of Ji and Bi Gan were Zhou's uncles (紂諸父). Seeing Zhou without the Way, the Viscount of Wei left him so that the ancestral sacrifices would go on (去之以存宗祀); the other two remonstrated; Zhou killed Bi Gan and imprisoned the Viscount of Ji as a slave, and the Viscount of Ji then feigned madness and bore the disgrace (箕子因佯狂而受辱). Ma Rong in He Yan tells it in much the same way. 為 wéi 'to become'; 之奴 'his slave'. 諫而死 'remonstrated and died': 而 joins two verbs, here an act and what came of it. Variant: He Yan's text prints 比于 for 比干, though Ma Rong's comment beside it has 比干 — most likely a slip of that print.

sentences.t: 孔子曰：「殷有三仁焉。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l: Kongzi said: “The Yin had three humane men.”
sentences.i: Kongzi said: “In the Yin there were three men of humaneness.”
sentences.n: 殷 Yin is the Shang dynasty (2.23). 仁 here stands for men who have humaneness, as at 1.6. 焉 yān at the end is the fused 於之 'in it': 'there were three humane men in it', in the Yin. Kongzi gives the verdict without saying whose course was best. Zhu Xi: the three acted differently, but all from the same utmost sincerity and heartfelt grief (至誠惻怛之意), so none went against the principle of love and each kept whole the virtue of his heart; he quotes Yang Shi: each kept his original heart, so all alike are called humane. He Yan's own comment (unsigned): the humane love others; the three acted differently and are alike called humane because all were anxious over the disorder and wanted peace for the people (以其俱在憂亂寧民也).

sentences.t:
栁下惠為士師，三黜。
人曰：「子未可以去乎？」
曰：「
直道而事人，焉往而不三黜？
枉道而事人，何必去父母之邦？」

morph.gloss: the willow (the edition's form of 柳), in the name 栁下惠 (15.13)
a favour, kindness, a benefit bestowed

sentences.l:
Liuxia Hui served as officer of justice and was three times dismissed.
Someone said: “Can you not leave yet, sir?”
He said:
“Keeping the way straight and serving others, where could I go and not be three times dismissed?
Bending the way and serving others, why must I leave the state of my father and mother?”
sentences.i: Liuxia Hui was officer of justice and was put out of office three times. Someone said to him: “Is it not time you left this state?” He answered: “If I serve men without bending my way, where could I go and not be put out three times over? And if I were willing to bend it, why should I need to leave my parents' country?”
sentences.n: 栁 is the edition's form of 柳; Liuxia Hui is the grandee of Lu of 15.13. 為 wéi 'to serve as'. 士師 'officer of justice': Zhu Xi 士師獄官, the officer over trials and prisons; Kong Anguo in He Yan 典獄之官. 黜 chù 'to put out of office' (Zhu Xi: 黜退也). 三 'three times': Zhu Xi marks it 去聲 (sàn, the old reading for 'thrice'); we print sān, as at 5.19. 子 'you, sir', polite address. 未可以去乎 'can you not yet leave?' — is it not time to go to another state? 焉 is yān 'where' (Zhu Xi: 於虔反). In 直道而事人, 而 joins the manner to the act: 'keeping the way straight, (to) serve others'. Both halves of the answer are rhetorical questions: wherever he went, the straight way would get him dismissed; and if he would bend it, he could keep office at home. 父母之邦 'the state of father and mother', his own country. Zhu Xi: thrice dismissed and not leaving, and answering so calmly (其辭氣雍容如此), he can be called at ease (和); yet his refusal to bend the Way stood firm, not to be uprooted (確乎其不可拔者). He quotes Hu Yin: there must once have been words of Kongzi judging this, now lost (此必有孔子斷之之言而亡之矣). Kong Anguo in He Yan: if he serves men by the straight way, in whatever state he goes to he will again be dismissed three times.

sentences.t:
齊景公待孔子，曰：「
若季氏，則吾不能；
以季孟之閒待之。」
曰：「吾老矣，不能用也。」
孔子行。

morph.gloss: to make even, to bring to one standard (Zhu Xi: 所以一之也)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
Ji, the clan name (Jisun) of the Lu house
clan, house (the family name as a lineage)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Duke Jing of Qi, on how to receive Kongzi, said:
“As for (treating him) like the Ji, that I cannot;
I will receive him between the Ji and the Meng.”
He said: “I am old; I am not able to make use of him.”
Kongzi left.
sentences.i: Duke Jing of Qi, considering how he should receive Kongzi, said: “To treat him as the Ji are treated in Lu is more than I can do; I shall put him somewhere between the Ji and the Meng.” Later he said: “I am an old man now; I am in no position to employ him.” Kongzi left Qi.
sentences.n: 齊景公 is Duke Jing of Qi (12.11, 16.12). 待 'to receive, to treat (a guest)'. 若季氏則… '(treating him) like the Ji — that…': 若 is 'like, as', and 則 sets off what the duke says of it. 季氏 the Ji and 孟 the Meng are two of the three great houses of Lu (3.1, 16.1). Zhu Xi: of Lu's three ministerial houses the Ji were the most honoured and the Meng the lowest (魯三卿季氏最貴孟氏為下卿); Kong Anguo in He Yan: the Ji were the senior minister, the Meng a junior minister without charge of affairs (不用事), so the duke meant to treat him between the two. 閒 is the edition's form of 間 jiān 'between'. The second 曰 is still the duke, later. 不能用 'not able to use (him)': the object is left out, as so often. 行 xíng 'to go away, to leave' — Zhu Xi: Kongzi left him, as the Shiji's account of his house tells (事見世家). Zhu Xi adds that these were surely not words said to Kongzi's face: the duke said them to his own ministers and Kongzi heard of them (此言必非面語孔子葢自以告其臣而孔子聞之爾). He quotes Master Cheng: the Ji were an overmighty minister whom their lord treated with the highest courtesy; to treat Kongzi between Ji and Meng was courtesy enough — but the duke then said 'I am old, I cannot use him', and so Kongzi left, not over how lightly or heavily he was received, only because he would not be used (特以不用而去爾). He Yan's own comment: the duke said this because the sage's Way is hard to bring to completion (以聖道難成故云老矣不能用).

sentences.t:
齊人歸女樂，
季桓子受之，三日不朝。
孔子行。

morph.gloss: Ji Huanzi — head of the Ji house
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: Qi made Lu a gift of women musicians. Ji Huanzi accepted them, and for three days the court did not sit. Kongzi left.
sentences.n: 歸 guī 'to send as a gift', as at 17.1, and again Zhu Xi notes 歸如字或作饋: read it as written, though some texts write 饋 'to present' (read kuì). 女樂 'women's music': women musicians and dancers; 女 nǚ, 樂 yuè. 季桓子 Ji Huanzi — Zhu Xi: a grandee of Lu named Si (季桓子魯大夫名斯), head of the Ji house (the Ji Huanzi whom Yang Huo imprisoned, 17.1). 朝 is cháo 'court, to hold or attend court' (Zhu Xi: 朝音潮); 不朝 leaves open who stayed away. Zhu Xi cites the Shiji: Kongzi was then minister of justice of Lu and acting chief minister (孔子為魯司寇攝行相事); Qi took fright and sent the women musicians to block him (齊人懼歸女樂以沮之). The print dates it 定公四十年, 'Duke Ding's fortieth year' — evidently for 十四年, the fourteenth, since Duke Ding did not reign forty years. He quotes Yin Tun: to accept them and neglect government like this showed a man who slighted worth and cast off the rites, with whom nothing could be done, so the Master left — what the Book of Changes calls seeing the first sign and acting, not waiting for the day to end (見幾而作不俟終日). And Fan Zuyu: this book records the comings and goings of the humane and the worthy and measures them by the sage's conduct, to make clear the Way of the mean (中庸之道). Kong Anguo in He Yan: Huanzi made Duke Ding accept the women; ruler and minister watched them together and gave up the rites of court for three days (君臣相與觀之廢朝禮三日也).

sentences.t:
楚狂接輿歌而過孔子，曰：「
鳳兮鳳兮！何徳之衰！
往者不可諫，
來者猶可追。
已而，已而！
今之從政者殆而！」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The madman of Chu, Jieyu, passed Kongzi singing, saying:
“Phoenix, ah! phoenix, ah! How virtue has waned!
What is gone cannot be remonstrated with;
what is coming can still be caught up with.
Stop, then! stop, then!
Those who go into government now are in peril!”
sentences.i: Jieyu, the man of Chu who played the madman, went singing past Kongzi: “Phoenix, phoenix, how low your virtue has sunk! There is no pleading with what is past; what lies ahead may yet be overtaken. Let it be, let it be! Whoever takes up government in times like these puts himself at risk.”
sentences.n: Zhu Xi: Jieyu was a man of Chu who feigned madness to keep away from the world (接輿楚人佯狂辟世); the Master was about to go to Chu, so Jieyu sang as he passed in front of his carriage (歌而過其車前也). Kong Anguo in He Yan: he came singing in feigned madness, hoping to move Kongzi. 兮 xī is a lilt at the end of a sung phrase. The phoenix (9.8), Zhu Xi says, shows itself when the Way prevails and hides when it does not (鳳有道則見無道則隠); Jieyu likens Kongzi to it and mocks him for not hiding — that is the waning of virtue. 何徳之衰: 之 between subject and verb makes 'virtue wane' into a phrase, 'virtue's waning', and 何 'how' turns it into an exclamation. 者 makes nouns of 往 and 來: 'what has gone', 'what is to come'. Zhu Xi: 'what is coming can be caught up with' means it is still not too late to hide (言及今尚可隠去); 已 'to stop'; 而 is a filler particle (語助辭); 殆 'in danger' (殆危也). He adds that Jieyu evidently knew to honour Kongzi, though his course was different (葢知尊孔子而趣不同者也). Kong Anguo reads the lines the same way: what is past cannot be stopped by remonstrance; from now on one can still stop of oneself, avoid the disorder and live hidden; 已而 says the age is too far gone to be set right, and saying it twice is grief. Variants: He Yan's text reads 過孔子之門 'passed Kongzi's gate', and 何德之衰也, 往者不可諫也, 猶可追也, each with a final 也.

sentences.t:
孔子下，欲與之言。
趨而辟之，不得與之言。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Kongzi got down, wanting to talk with him.
He hurried off and avoided him; he did not get to talk with him.
sentences.i: Kongzi climbed down, hoping to talk with him, but the man hurried away out of his reach, and Kongzi never had his talk.
sentences.n: 下 'got down' — from his carriage (Zhu Xi: 孔子下車; Bao Xian in He Yan: 下下車也). 與之言 'to talk with him', 與 yǔ. 趨 qū 'to hurry'. 辟 is bì 'to avoid', the word later written 避 (Zhu Xi: 辟去聲; He Yan's text writes 避, as at 14.39). The subjects change without being named — Kongzi gets down, Jieyu hurries off, Kongzi fails to talk — and the reader supplies who does what. 不得 'did not get to'. Zhu Xi: Kongzi got down meaning to tell him his own mind on taking office and withdrawing (欲告之以出處之意); Jieyu thought himself right and did not want to hear it, so he kept away.

sentences.t:
長沮、桀溺耦而耕。
孔子過之，使子路問津焉。

morph.gloss: to check (here part of a name)
to sink, to soak (here part of a name)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Changju and Jieni were ploughing side by side.
Kongzi passed them, and had Zilu ask them about the ford.
sentences.i: Changju and Jieni were at the plough together, side by side. Kongzi, going by, sent Zilu to ask them where the river could be crossed.
sentences.n: 長沮 Changju and 桀溺 Jieni — Zhu Xi: both were recluses (二人隠者); Zheng Xuan in He Yan says the same. Readings: 沮 is jǔ in modern practice; Zhu Xi spells it 七余反, a level-tone reading (modern qū) — noted here once. 溺 is nì (乃歴反). 耦 ǒu 'in a pair': Zhu Xi 耦並耕也, two ploughing side by side; Zheng Xuan says a ploughshare was five inches wide and two shares made a 耦 (耜廣五寸二耜為耦). Zhu Xi: this was when Kongzi was coming back from Chu to Cai (時孔子自楚反乎蔡). 使 shǐ 'to have (someone do)'. 津 jīn is a ford, a crossing place (Zhu Xi and Zheng Xuan: 濟渡處). 焉 'of them' (the fused 於之).

sentences.t:
長沮曰：「夫執輿者為誰？」
子路曰：「為孔丘。」
曰：「是魯孔丘與？」
曰：「是也。」
曰：「是知津矣。」

morph.gloss: to check, to stop (齊人懼歸女樂以沮之, Zhu Xi on 18.4)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
Qiu: Confucius's own personal name (Kong Qiu 孔丘), used in speaking of himself

sentences.l:
Changju said: “That one holding the reins in the carriage — who is he?”
Zilu said: “It is Kong Qiu.”
He said: “Is it Kong Qiu of Lu?”
He said: “It is.”
He said: “Then he knows the ford.”
sentences.i: “And the man in the carriage with the reins in his hands — who is he?” asked Changju. “Kong Qiu,” said Zilu. “Kong Qiu of Lu?” “Yes.” “Then he knows where the ford is.”
sentences.n: 夫 is fú 'that' (Zhu Xi: 夫音扶). 執輿 'holding (the reins in) the carriage' — Zhu Xi: 執輿執轡在車也; Zilu had been driving and holding the reins, and now that he had got down to ask about the ford the Master took them in his place (葢本子路御而執轡今下問津故夫子代之也). 為 wéi 'to be': 為誰 'is who?', 為孔丘 '(it) is Kong Qiu'. Zilu names his master by surname and personal name, 孔丘 Kong Qiu (丘 is the name Kongzi uses of himself, 7.23). 是…與 'is this…?', 與 yú (Zhu Xi: 與平聲). 是知津矣 'this (man) knows the ford': 是 points back to Kong Qiu, and 矣 marks it as settled. Zhu Xi: he means that one who travels about so much must know the fords for himself (知津言數周流自知津處) — the gibe in the words is left for the reader to hear; Ma Rong in He Yan says the same. Variant: He Yan's text reads 對曰是也 'answered: It is.'

sentences.t:
問於桀溺。
桀溺曰：「子為誰？」
曰：「為仲由。」
曰：「是魯孔丘之徒與？」
對曰：「然。」
曰：「
滔滔者天下皆是也，而誰以易之？
且而與其從辟人之士也，豈若從辟世之士哉？」
耰而不輟。

morph.gloss: to sink, to soak, to drown (in 桀溺, 18.6)
to sink, to soak, to drown (in 桀溺, 18.6)
Zhong, the courtesy name of Guan Yiwu
Qiu: Confucius's own personal name (Kong Qiu 孔丘), used in speaking of himself

sentences.l:
He asked Jieni.
Jieni said: “Who are you?”
He said: “I am Zhong You.”
He said: “Kong Qiu of Lu's follower?”
He answered: “So it is.”
He said:
“Surging on and away — all under Heaven is like this; and with whom will you change it?
Besides, you — rather than follow a man who avoids people, how would that compare with following a man who avoids the age?”
He covered the seed and did not stop.
sentences.i: Then he asked Jieni. “Who are you?” said Jieni. “Zhong You.” “The one who follows Kong Qiu of Lu?” “I am.” “All under Heaven is a torrent pouring off, never to come back — and who is there to change it with? As for you: instead of following a man who keeps clear of this or that person, why not follow one who keeps clear of the whole age?” And he kept raking earth over his seed and never stopped.
sentences.n: 仲由 Zhong You is Zilu's own name (6.6), given plainly, as Kongzi's was. 是…之徒與 'a follower of …?', 與 yú (Zhu Xi: 徒與之與平聲). 對 'to answer', of a formal reply. 滔滔 tāo tāo (Zhu Xi: 滔土刀反) — Zhu Xi: water flowing away and never coming back (滔滔流而不反之意): the whole world is in disorder (天下皆亂). Kong Anguo in He Yan takes 滔滔 as 'going round everywhere' (周流之貌): order and disorder are the same the world over, so why leave this place for that one? 以 here means 'with' (Zhu Xi: 以猶與也): 誰以易之 'with whom will you change it?'. And 而 in 且而 is 'you' (Zhu Xi: 而汝也), not 'and'. 與其…豈若… 'rather than…, how could it compare with…?', 與 yǔ. 辟 bì 'to avoid' (= 避; Zhu Xi 辟去聲). Zhu Xi: the man who avoids people is Kongzi, who leaves one ruler for another; the man who avoids the age is Jieni himself (辟人謂孔子辟世桀溺自謂). He Yan's unsigned comment: there is a way of avoiding people and a way of avoiding the age. 耰 yōu (Zhu Xi: 音憂) 'to cover the seed with earth' (Zhu Xi and Zheng Xuan: 耰覆種也); 輟 chuò 'to stop' (Zheng Xuan: 輟止也). Zhu Xi: he, too, did not tell him where the ford was (亦不告以津處). Variants: He Yan's text writes 避 for 辟, and reads 從避人之士 without the 也.

sentences.t:
子路行以告。
夫子憮然曰：「
鳥獸不可與同羣，
吾非斯人之徒與，而誰與？
天下有道，丘不與易也。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zilu went on and reported it.
The Master, rueful, said:
“Birds and beasts — one cannot share a flock with them.
If not with the company of these people, then with whom?
If the world had the Way, I, Qiu, would not join in changing it.”
sentences.i: Zilu went on and told the Master, who was saddened. “A man cannot go off and live in a flock among the birds and the beasts. These men are my own kind: if I do not keep among them, among whom am I to keep? Were the Way at work in the world, there would be nothing for me, Qiu, to join in changing.”
sentences.n: 憮 wǔ (Zhu Xi: 憮音武); 憮然 'rueful' — Zhu Xi: like 悵然 'disappointed', regretting that they had not understood his meaning (惜其不喻己意也); He Yan's unsigned comment: because they had not grasped his meaning and simply condemned him. Every 與 here is yǔ (Zhu Xi: 與如字 — read as written, not as the question particle): 'with, to keep company with' in the first three, 'to take part in' in the last: 不可與同羣 'one cannot flock together with (them)'; 吾非斯人之徒與 'if I do not keep with the company of these people'; 而誰與 'then with whom?'; 不與易 'would not join in changing (it)'. 羣 is the edition's form of 群. Zhu Xi: those one ought to flock with are these people and no others (所當與同羣者斯人而已); how could one cut oneself off from men and flee the world and call that being clean (豈可絶人逃世以為潔哉)? If the world were already at peace and in order I would have no use for changing it; it is just because the world lacks the Way that I wish to change it by the Way. He quotes Master Cheng: the sage dares not have a heart that forgets the world; and Zhang Zai: the sage's humaneness does not give up on the world for lacking the Way. Kong Anguo in He Yan: to live hidden in the hills and forests is to flock with birds and beasts; I should keep company with the people of this world — how could I leave men to live with birds and beasts? 丘 Qiu: the Master names himself, as at 7.23. 天下有道 'the world has the Way' (16.2). Variant: He Yan's text reads 鳥獸不可與同羣也, with a final 也.

sentences.t:
子路從而後，遇丈人，以杖荷蓧。
子路問曰：「子見夫子乎？」
丈人曰：「
四體不勤，五榖不分，
孰為夫子？」
植其杖而芸。

(a measure of ten feet; an elder)

sentences.l:
Zilu, following, fell behind, and met an elder carrying a bamboo basket on his shoulder by a staff.
Zilu asked: “Have you seen my master, sir?”
The elder said:
“Four limbs not toiling, five grains not told apart —
who is your master?”
He stood his staff in the ground and weeded.
sentences.i: Zilu, travelling in the Master's company, had dropped behind. He came upon an old man with a bamboo basket hung from the staff across his shoulder. “Have you seen my master, sir?” Zilu asked. The old man said: “Never a day's toil for those four limbs, and you wouldn't know beans from wheat — who is this master of yours?” And he stuck his staff in the ground and set to weeding.
sentences.n: 從而後 'following, fell behind': 從 cóng; 後 hòu used as a verb. 丈人 'an elder' — Zhu Xi: another recluse (丈人亦隠者); Bao Xian in He Yan: an old man (丈人老者也). 荷 hè 'to carry on the shoulder' (as 14.42); 以杖荷蓧 'by a staff shouldered a basket': the basket hung from the staff. 蓧 diào (Zhu Xi: 徒弔反) is a bamboo vessel (Zhu Xi 竹器; Bao Xian 竹器名). 見 jiàn 'to see'. 夫子 is 'my master' in Zilu's mouth and 'your master' in the old man's. 四體 'the four limbs'; 勤 qín 'to toil'; 五榖 'the five grains' (榖 is the edition's form of 穀 gǔ); 分 fēn 'to tell apart' (Zhu Xi: 分辨也). Zhu Xi: 'not telling the five grains apart' is like saying 'cannot tell beans from wheat' (猶言不辨菽麥爾) — the old man is rebuking Zilu for not working the land and following a teacher far from home (責其不事農業而従師逺遊也). Bao Xian reads it as rebuke too, but takes 分 as 'to plant out' (不分殖五穀) and the last words as 'who is your master, that you look for him?' (誰為夫子而索之耶). 為 wéi 'to be'. 植 zhí (Zhu Xi: 植音值) 'to set upright' (植立之也); Kong Anguo in He Yan takes it as 'to lean (it against something)' (植倚也). 芸 yún 'to weed' (Zhu Xi: 芸去草也; Kong Anguo: 除草曰芸).

sentences.t: 子路拱而立。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l: Zilu stood with his hands clasped.
sentences.i: Zilu stood there, his hands joined before him in respect.
sentences.n: 拱 gǒng is to join the hands in front of the chest, a gesture of respect. 而 links the manner to the act: 'clasping his hands, stood'. Zhu Xi: he knew him for a recluse and showed him respect (知其隠者敬之也). He Yan's unsigned comment reads it otherwise: Zilu did not know what to answer (未知所以答也).

sentences.t:
止子路宿，
殺雞為黍而食之，
見其二子焉。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
He kept Zilu to stay the night,
killed a chicken and made millet and fed him,
and presented his two sons to him.
sentences.i: He kept Zilu for the night, killed a chicken and cooked millet to feed him, and brought out his two sons to meet him.
sentences.n: 止 'to stop, to detain': 止子路宿 'kept Zilu (to) stay the night', 宿 sù. 殺 shā 'to kill'. 為黍 'made millet': 為 wéi 'to make, to prepare'; 黍 shǔ is millet. 食 is sì 'to feed', and 見 is xiàn 'to present, to bring before' (Zhu Xi: 食音嗣見賢遍反). 焉 'to him' (= 於之). The old man is the subject throughout, never named: the sense alone tells you. The two sons matter in what follows: by presenting them, Zhu Xi says, the old man showed he knew the order between elder and younger must be kept (unit 15).

sentences.t:
明日，子路行以告。
子曰：「隠者也。」
使子路反見之。
至，則行矣。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Next day Zilu went on and reported it.
The Master said: “He is a recluse.”
He had Zilu go back to see him.
When he arrived, he had gone.
sentences.i: Next day Zilu went on and told the Master. “He is a man in hiding,” said the Master, and sent Zilu back to find him; but by the time Zilu reached the place, the old man was no longer there.
sentences.n: 明日 'the next day'. 隠 is the edition's form of 隱; 隠者 'one who hides', a recluse. 使 shǐ 'to have (someone do)'; 反 'to go back'; 見 jiàn 'to see'. 至則行矣 'arrived, and (he had) gone': 則 marks what Zilu found, and 矣 that it was already done. Zhu Xi: Kongzi sent Zilu back meaning to tell the old man what is right between lord and minister (欲告之以君臣之義); the old man guessed Zilu would come again and left first to wipe out his tracks — the same mind as Jieyu's (亦接輿之意也). Kong Anguo in He Yan: when Zilu got to his house, the old man had gone out and was not there (丈人出行不在).

sentences.t:
子路曰：「
不仕無義。
長幼之節，不可廢也；
君臣之義，如之何其廢之？
欲潔其身，而亂大倫。
君子之仕也，行其義也。
道之不行，已知之矣。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
to be like, to come up to
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zilu said:
“Not to take office is to lack what is right.
The order between elder and younger cannot be cast aside;
what is right between lord and minister — how could that be cast aside?
Wishing to keep oneself clean, one throws the great order into disorder.
A gentleman's taking office is doing what is right.
That the Way does not prevail — that is known already.”
sentences.i: Zilu said: “To refuse office is to fail in what is right. He would not let the order between old and young be set aside — how then can he set aside what is owed between lord and subject? Wanting to keep himself unsoiled, he throws the great bonds between men into disorder. When a gentleman takes office, it is to do what is right. That the Way is not going to prevail, he knows already.”
sentences.n: Whom is Zilu speaking to? The old man is gone. Zheng Xuan in He Yan: Zilu left these words to be told to the old man's two sons (留言以語丈人之二子也). Zhu Xi: Zilu is setting out the Master's mind (子路述夫子之意如此); the old man had been very offhand with Zilu and Zilu all the more respectful, and by presenting his sons the old man showed he knew the order of elder and younger must not be given up — so Zilu reasons from what he already grasped. Zhu Xi also records that a manuscript from early in the dynasty at Fuzhou has 反子 after 子路 — 'Zilu came back, and the Master said' — which would make these the Master's words; he does not know if it is right (未知是否). 長 zhǎng 'elder' (Zhu Xi: 長上聲). 節 'proper measure, order'. 如之何其廢之 'how could one cast it aside?': 如之何 'how' (2.20), and 其 adds 'could one'. Kong Anguo in He Yan: you know that father and son must care for each other and that cannot be given up — can you then give up what is right between lord and minister? 而 'and yet', setting the aim against the result. 倫 lún 'order' (Zhu Xi: 倫序也; Bao Xian: 倫道也理也); Zhu Xi lists the five great orders of men — affection between father and son, right between lord and minister, distinction between husband and wife, precedence between elder and younger, good faith between friends — a list also found in the Mencius. 也…也 sets out a definition: 'a gentleman's taking office is doing what is right'. Zhu Xi: taking office is how the right between lord and minister is carried out, so even knowing the Way will not prevail one may not give it up; yet because it is a matter of right, one does not take or leave office carelessly either — not cleaning oneself at the cost of the order, nor forgetting the right to chase a salary (亦非忘義以徇禄也). 已 yǐ 'already'. Variants: He Yan's text reads 如之何其可廢也 'how could it be cast aside?' (adding 可, with 也 for 之) and 道之不行也已知之矣 (adding 也).

sentences.t:
逸民：
伯夷、叔齊、虞仲、夷逸、
朱張、栁下惠、少連。

morph.gloss: the Yi, the peoples of the east
to make even, to bring to one standard (Zhu Xi: 所以一之也)
left out (here part of a name)
the willow (the edition's form of 柳), in the name 栁下惠 (15.13)
a favour, kindness, a benefit bestowed
to join (here part of a name)

sentences.l:
Men left out of office:
Boyi, Shuqi, Yu Zhong, Yi Yi,
Zhu Zhang, Liuxia Hui, Shao Lian.
sentences.i: Men of worth who lived out of office: Boyi, Shuqi, Yu Zhong, Yi Yi, Zhu Zhang, Liuxia Hui and Shao Lian.
sentences.n: 逸 yì; 逸民 — Zhu Xi: 逸 is 'left out, passed over' (遺逸), and 民 is the name for those who hold no rank (民者無位之稱). He Yan's unsigned comment: men whose conduct rose clear above the common (節行超逸者); Bao Xian: these seven were all men of worth among them (此七人皆逸民之賢者也). Boyi and Shuqi are the brothers of 5.22, 7.14 and 16.12; Liuxia Hui is the grandee of 15.13 and 18.2. Zhu Xi: Yu Zhong is Zhongyong, who fled to the Jing Man in the south with his brother Taibo (虞仲即仲雍與泰伯同竄荆蠻者; 8.1); Yi Yi and Zhu Zhang appear in no classic or commentary (不見經傳); Shao Lian was a man of the Eastern Yi (東夷人). 少 is read shào here and in 少師 (18.9; Zhu Xi: 少去聲下同). The list names seven; the next units, in the Master's voice, take up all but Zhu Zhang.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
不降其志，不辱其身，
伯夷、叔齊與！」

morph.gloss: the Yi, the peoples of the east
to make even, to bring to one standard (Zhu Xi: 所以一之也)

sentences.l:
The Master said:
“Not lowering their aims, not disgracing their persons —
surely, Boyi and Shuqi!”
sentences.i: The Master said: “They never let their aims sink, and never let shame touch them — that was Boyi and Shuqi.”
sentences.n: 降 jiàng 'to lower'; 辱 'to disgrace'; 志 'aim, what the heart is set on'. The description comes first and the names after, closed by 與 yú (Zhu Xi: 與平聲), a judgment put gently: 'that would be Boyi and Shuqi'. Zheng Xuan in He Yan: they kept their hearts straight and would not enter the court of a common ruler (言其直己之心不入庸君之朝). The Master's words run on past Zhu Xi's comments through units 18–20. Variant: He Yan's text reads 不辱其身者 'those who did not disgrace their persons', adding 者.

sentences.t:
謂栁下惠、少連：「
降志辱身矣；
言中倫，行中慮，
其斯而已矣。」

morph.gloss: the willow (the edition's form of 柳), in the name 栁下惠 (15.13)
a favour, kindness, a benefit bestowed

sentences.l:
Of Liuxia Hui and Shao Lian he said:
“They lowered their aims and disgraced their persons;
their words hit the proper order, their conduct hit what is well considered —
this, and that is all.”
sentences.i: Of Liuxia Hui and Shao Lian he said: “They let their aims sink and suffered shame in their persons; but what they said kept to the proper order of things, and what they did answered to careful thought. That much, and no more.”
sentences.n: 謂 'to say of' (as 孔子謂季氏, 3.1): the Master is still speaking. 中 is zhòng 'to hit (the mark), to accord with', here and in the next unit (Zhu Xi: 中去聲下同). 倫 is the order of what is right and reasonable (倫義理之次第也), and 慮 'thought' (慮思慮也): 中慮 means their acts had meaning and satisfied people's minds (中慮言有意義合人心). 行 here is the noun 'conduct', given the modern reading xíng. 其斯而已矣 'they — this, and that is all': 而已矣 'and no more'. Zhu Xi: Liuxia Hui's story is above (18.2); Shao Lian's cannot be traced, but the Record (記, the Record of Rites) praises him as good at mourning — not slack for three days, not remiss for three months, grieving a full year and sorrowing three years (三日不怠三月不解期悲哀三年憂) — from which his 'hitting what is considered' can be seen. Kong Anguo in He Yan: they could only make their words answer to the proper order and their conduct to careful thought, no more than this (若此而已).

sentences.t:
謂虞仲、夷逸：「
隠居，放言，
身中清，廢中權。」

morph.gloss: Yu, the name of Shun's reign (Zhu Xi: 唐虞，堯舜有天下之號)
Zhong, the courtesy name of Guan Yiwu
the Yi, the peoples of the east
left out, passed over (in 逸民, 夷逸, 18.8)

sentences.i: Of Yu Zhong and Yi Yi he said: “They lived in hiding and spoke without restraint; in their persons they stayed clean, and in stepping aside they weighed the times rightly.”
sentences.n: 隠居 'to dwell hidden' (16.11). 放 fàng 'to let go'. 中 zhòng 'to hit', as in the last unit. 權 quán is the weight of a steelyard, and so the weighing of things (9.29): here, a choice fitted to the times. Zhu Xi: Zhongyong (Yu Zhong) lived in Wu, cut his hair, tattooed his body, and went naked for ornament (仲雍居吳斷髮文身裸以為飾); living hidden and keeping good on their own fitted the purity of the Way, and speaking freely and setting themselves aside fitted the Way's weighing (隠居獨善合乎道之清放言自廢合乎道之權). Xie Liangzuo, whom Zhu Xi quotes at the end of the chapter, adds that much of what they said did not fit the rules of the former kings, but they were clean and unsoiled, and their weighing was fitting. The older readings take 放言 the other way: Bao Xian in He Yan glosses 放 as 'to set aside' — they put speech away and no longer talked of the world's affairs (放置也置不復言世務也). Ma Rong: 清 is pure and clean; in a disordered age they set themselves aside to escape harm, which accords with the weighing (遭世亂身廢棄以免患合於權也).

sentences.t:
我則異於是，
無可無不可。
sentences.l:
I, for my part, differ from these:
no 'may', no 'may not'.
sentences.i: As for me, I go another way: for me nothing is settled beforehand as allowed, and nothing as ruled out.
sentences.n: These are still the Master's words: the 子曰 of unit 17 runs on past Zhu Xi's comments, and since this unit opens with them and has no verb of saying, it is left unquoted. 我則 'I, for my part' — 則 sets him against the others. 異於是 'differ from these' (於 'from, than'). 無可無不可 'no “may”, no “may not”'. Zhu Xi explains it with Mencius: Kongzi took office when he could take office, stopped when he could stop, stayed long when he could stay long, left quickly when he could leave quickly (孔子可以仕則仕可以止則止可以久則久可以速則速); that is what 'no may, no may not' means. Ma Rong in He Yan: not bound to go forward, not bound to withdraw — only where the right lies (亦不必進亦不必退唯義所在). Zhu Xi quotes Xie Liangzuo ranking the seven: Boyi and Shuqi, whom the Son of Heaven could not make ministers nor the lords make friends, stand highest, one step below the sage; Liuxia Hui and Shao Lian lowered their aims but never bent themselves; Yu Zhong and Yi Yi strayed in speech but were clean and weighed rightly — unlike the men 'beyond the bounds' (方外之士) who harm the right and throw the great order into disorder. And Yin Tun: the seven each kept to a single principle, while Kongzi had no fixed 'may' or 'may not', and so always met what was fitting (常適其可).

sentences.t: 大師摯適齊。
sentences.l: The Grand Music-Master Zhi went to Qi.
sentences.i: Zhi, the Grand Music-Master, left for Qi.
sentences.n: This chapter lists the court musicians of Lu who scattered. 大 is read tài (Zhu Xi: 大音泰): 大師, the Grand Music-Master (3.23), was the head of the music officers of Lu, and 摯 Zhi was his name (大師魯樂官之長摯其名也) — the 師摯 of 8.15. 適 shì 'to go to'. Each musician here is named by his post and then his own name; the post is kept as one word and the name stands beside it. Zhu Xi: this records worthy men going into hiding and is set after the chapter before, though it is not necessarily the Master's words (此記賢人之隠遁以附前章然未必夫子之言也; and so with the last chapter). He quotes Zhang Zai: when Zhou declined and music was neglected, the Master came back from Wei to Lu and once set it in order (9.14); afterwards even players and humble musicians knew correct music, and when Lu declined further and the three Huan houses overreached, all from the Grand Music-Master down knew to scatter in every direction, crossing the River and taking to the sea to leave the disorder — such was the effect of the sage's brief help. Kong Anguo in He Yan, at the end of the chapter, places it in the time of Duke Ai of Lu, when the rites were ruined and music collapsed (魯哀公時禮毀樂崩).

sentences.t:
亞飯干適楚，
三飯繚適蔡，
四飯缺適秦。
sentences.i: Gan, who played at the second meal, left for Chu; Liao, who played at the third, for Cai; Que, who played at the fourth, for Qin.
sentences.n: 亞 yà 'second, next' (Kong Anguo: 亞次也). 飯 fàn 'a meal' (Zhu Xi spells it 扶晚反, which modern practice reads fàn). Zhu Xi: from 亞飯 on, these are officers who played music to encourage the ruler as he ate (以樂侑食之官), and 干, 繚, 缺 are names (干繚缺皆名也). Kong Anguo: the musician of the second meal (次飯樂師也). Bao Xian in He Yan takes 三飯 and 四飯 as the names of pieces of music, each with its own master (三飯四飯樂章名也各異師). 繚 is liǎo (Zhu Xi: 繚音了); 缺 quē. Chu, Cai and Qin are other states, like Qi.

sentences.t: 鼓方叔入於河。
sentences.l: The drummer Fang Shu went in to the River.
sentences.i: Fang Shu the drummer went off to the land by the River.
sentences.n: 鼓 'a drum' here stands for the one who beats it (Zhu Xi: 鼓擊鼓者; Bao Xian the same), and 方叔 Fang Shu is his name. 入於河 'went in to the River': Zhu Xi glosses 河 as 河内, the land 'within the River', by the Yellow River; Bao Xian says 入 means he went to live there (入謂居其河內也).

sentences.t: 播鼗武入於漢。
sentences.l: Wu, who shook the hand-drum, went in to the Han.
sentences.i: Wu, who played the twirling drum, went to the country of the Han.
sentences.n: 播 bō 'to shake, to twirl' (Zhu Xi: 播搖也; Kong Anguo: 播猶搖也). 鼗 táo (Zhu Xi: 徒刀反) — Zhu Xi: a small drum with an ear on either side; you hold it by the handle and twirl it, and the ears swing round and strike it (鼗小鼓兩旁有耳持其柄而搖之則旁耳還自擊). 武 Wu is his name (武名也). 漢 Han: Zhu Xi 漢中, the country of the Han River. The words before the name say what the man did, as 鼓 'the drummer' does in the last unit.

sentences.t:
少師陽、
擊磬襄入於海。
sentences.l:
The Assistant Music-Master Yang,
and Xiang, who struck the chime-stones, went in to the sea.
sentences.i: Yang, the Assistant Music-Master, and Xiang, who played the chime-stones, went off to the sea.
sentences.n: 少 is shào (Zhu Xi: 少去聲): 少師 is the Assistant Music-Master, the deputy among the music officers (少師樂官之佐), and 陽 Yang and 襄 Xiang are both names (陽襄二人名). Zhu Xi: Xiang is the man from whom Kongzi learned the zither (襄即孔子所従學琴者). 擊磬 'striking the chime-stones' (14.42). 海 'the sea' — Zhu Xi: an island in the sea (海島也). Kong Anguo in He Yan: in the time of Duke Ai of Lu the rites were ruined and music collapsed, and the musicians all left; Yang and Xiang are names.

sentences.t:
周公謂魯公曰：「
君子不施其親，
不使大臣怨乎不以；
故舊無大故，則不棄也；
無求備於一人。」

morph.gloss: the Duke of Lu — Bo Qin, the Duke of Zhou's son
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the old, what is past (故者舊所聞, 'what one heard of old')

sentences.i: The Duke of Zhou said to the Duke of Lu: “A gentleman does not neglect his own kin. He does not leave his great ministers aggrieved that he makes no use of them. He does not cast off old associates unless they have done something very wrong. Do not expect one man to have every gift.”
sentences.n: 周公 is the Duke of Zhou (7.5); 魯公, the Duke of Lu, is his son Bo Qin 伯禽 (Zhu Xi: 魯公周公子伯禽也; Kong Anguo in He Yan: enfeoffed in Lu). Zhu Xi quotes Hu Yin: these are the words of instruction the Duke of Zhou gave Bo Qin when he went to his fief, which the people of Lu recited and never forgot; perhaps the Master once spoke of them with his disciples. 施: Zhu Xi records that Lu Deming's text writes 弛, and so does the Fuzhou text (施陸氏本作弛福本同), and glosses 弛 as 'to neglect, to cast off' (弛遺棄也); we translate on his reading and print the character as written, read shī (he gives no sound). Ruan Yuan's 1816 edition prints 弛 in the text. Kong Anguo in He Yan reads 施 as 'to change, to put in place of' (施易也): the gentleman does not put others in the place of his kin. 以 'to use' (Zhu Xi and Kong Anguo: 以用也); 怨乎不以 'resent at not (being) used' — 乎 here is 'at, over' (= 於). Zhu Xi: if a great minister is not the right man, remove him; if he holds the post, he must not go unused. 故舊 'old associates' (8.2); 大故 'a grave cause' — Zhu Xi and Kong Anguo: grave wrongdoing or treason (惡逆). 無 here is 'do not' (= 毋), and 求備 'to demand completeness' (13.25). A Mr Li in Zhu Xi: all four are the gentleman's concern, the height of wholehearted generosity (忠厚之至也). Variants: He Yan's text reads 語魯公 'told the Duke of Lu' for 謂魯公, and 母求備 — 母 there is probably a slip for 毋 'do not', the same word as 無 here.

sentences.t:
周有八士：
伯達、伯适、
仲突、仲忍、
叔夜、叔夏、
季隨、季騧。
sentences.l:
Zhou had eight officers:
Bo Da, Bo Kuo,
Zhong Tu, Zhong Ren,
Shu Ye, Shu Xia,
Ji Sui, Ji Gua.
sentences.i: Zhou had eight officers: Bo Da and Bo Kuo, Zhong Tu and Zhong Ren, Shu Ye and Shu Xia, Ji Sui and Ji Gua.
sentences.n: 伯, 仲, 叔, 季 are the ranks of birth among brothers — eldest, second, third, youngest — so the names come in four pairs. Zhu Xi reports two views of their date, some saying they lived under King Cheng, some under King Xuan; it seems one mother bore twins four times, eight sons (葢一母四乳而生八子也), but it cannot be checked (然不可考矣). Bao Xian in He Yan: in Zhou times four births gave eight sons, all distinguished officers, so they were recorded. Zhang Zai: it records how many good men there were (記善人之多也). 适 is kuò, as in 南宫适 (14.6). 騧 guā; Zhu Xi spells it 烏瓜反, which points to wā — noted here once. Zhu Xi closes the book with a reflection of his own (愚按): Kongzi praised and ranked the three humane men, the men left out, Music Master Zhi and the eight officers, and showed again and again his eagerness to draw in Jieyu, Changju and Jieni and the old man (惓惓接引之意) — all the mind of a declining age, deeply felt. Had those lofty men heard the sage's Way, to trim their excess and push them where they fell short, how much further might they have gone! Variant: Ruan Yuan's edition and He Yan's text both read 仲忽 for 仲忍.
